scenes.title: What does this slope actually mean?
scenes.narration: A line passes through one comma two and four comma eight. What is its slope, and what does that number actually mean? Here’s the idea: slope is not just a formula. It measures how much y changes for each unit that x changes.

scenes.title: Match the changes
body: Do NOT reverse only one subtraction
scenes.narration: From the first point to the second, y rises from two to eight, so delta y is six. At the same time, x moves from one to four, so delta x is three. This is where students often mix things up: the subtraction order must match. If you reverse both changes, the negatives cancel and the slope is still correct. If you reverse only one, you create the wrong sign.

scenes.title: Rise over run is a rate
body: Meaning: +2 in y for every +1 in x
scenes.narration: Now divide the vertical change by the horizontal change: six over three equals two. Notice why this works. Over a run of three, the line rises six, so each one unit of horizontal movement corresponds to two units of vertical movement. Slope is the rate of that change.

scenes.title: See the rate on the graph
scenes.narration: We can check that directly on the line. Starting at one comma two, move right one and up two: you reach two comma four. Repeat it to three comma six, then four comma eight. The same rate repeats because a straight line has constant slope.

scenes.title: Read slope as meaning, not a slogan
body: Positive → line rises to the right
Slope = change in y per change in x
scenes.narration: So the slope is two, and the positive sign matches a line that rises as you move right. The key idea is to compare the change in y with the matching change in x, using the same direction for both. Then interpret the result as a rate, not just a number.
